#4478. New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss

An experimental electronic implant could offer an entirely new way to treat type 2 diabetes. Rather than relying on insulin or conventional medications, the device uses electricity to convert excess blood sugar into a substance that the body can eliminate. In early tests with diabetic mice, the technology successfully regulated blood sugar and also led to weight loss.

The development comes as type 2 diabetes continues to affect a growing number of people worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, type 2 is frequently associated with obesity, limited physical activity, and consuming more energy than the body needs over long periods.

Insulin injections can help reduce blood sugar by allowing muscle cells to absorb glucose from the bloodstream. However, insulin does not eliminate the underlying problem of excess energy. When the body does not use the glucose it absorbs, the surplus can eventually be converted into fat. This helps explain why some people with diabetes continue gaining weight even while receiving treatment.

Researchers led by Martin Fussenegger, a professor in the Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering at ETH Zurich in Basel, have developed an implant designed to address this problem differently. Their findings were published in the journal Science.

A New Diabetes Treatment Powered by Electricity

Fussenegger and his colleagues have spent years developing technologies capable of controlling blood sugar. Their previous designs used engineered genetic networks, but these systems depended on living cells and other biological materials.

That dependence introduced several complications. Biological components can create challenges involving immune compatibility, long-term stability, production, and regulatory approval.

The researchers have now taken a different approach by creating a catalyst made entirely from inorganic materials. It performs its function without requiring living cells, enzymes, or other biological components.

At the heart of the implant is a piece of graphite felt covered with tiny clusters of gold. These gold structures are coated with even smaller platinum particles, creating a specially engineered surface that enables the chemical reaction needed to process glucose.

The researchers designed this nanoscale surface themselves. According to Fussenegger, the materials also demonstrated excellent biocompatibility during experimental testing, suggesting they can interact with living tissue without causing significant adverse reactions.

The system includes an electronic controller enclosed in a 3D-printed housing. Instead of relying on a conventional wired power connection, the implant receives energy wirelessly at a frequency of 13.56 MHz. This frequency is internationally allocated for industrial, scientific, and medical applications.

How the Implant Removes Excess Blood Sugar

The technology works by transforming excess glucose into gluconate, a substance that can be eliminated from the body through urine.

Normally, glucose provides energy for cells. When more glucose is available than the body needs, some of that excess energy can ultimately be stored as fat. By converting part of the glucose into gluconate, the implant prevents that portion from being metabolized and stored in tissues, potentially helping reduce fat accumulation.

The entire process is designed to happen automatically, responding to changes in blood sugar as they occur.

A conventional glucose sensor, similar to those worn on the upper arm by many people with diabetes, continuously measures glucose concentrations in tissue. When levels rise too high, such as after a meal, the sensor communicates through Bluetooth with a smartphone or smartwatch.

The connected device then activates the implant, supplying the electrical energy needed for the catalyst to convert glucose into gluconate.

Once glucose levels return to the desired range, the implant automatically shuts down. This feedback system, known as closed-loop control, is intended to prevent blood sugar from dropping dangerously low.

Blood Sugar Control and Weight Loss in Diabetic Mice

To evaluate the technology, the researchers first conducted a laboratory experiment using a reservoir containing 5 liters of a nutrient solution with glucose. That volume is approximately equal to the amount of blood circulating in an adult human body.

The experiment demonstrated that the catalyst could convert glucose in a solution of this scale, an important step toward assessing its potential for medical applications.

The researchers then implanted the system in diabetic mice. The results showed that the device could precisely regulate the animals' blood sugar levels. The mice also lost weight, suggesting that converting excess glucose rather than allowing it to contribute to fat storage could offer an additional metabolic benefit.

Over six weeks of testing, the implant continued functioning reliably and was well tolerated by the animals.

"The system operates at a very low voltage, and our experiments showed no evidence of tissue damage from either electrical or thermal effects," says Fussenegger.

Although these findings are promising, the device has not yet been tested in humans. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the technology can operate safely and effectively in people with diabetes.

Could Electronics Transform the Future of Diabetes Treatment?

Fussenegger believes the technology could represent a fundamental change in how diabetes is managed. Rather than using medications to influence how the body processes glucose, an electronic device could directly control the amount of glucose available.

"For decades, we have treated diabetes by telling the body how to manage glucose. We are now showing that we can take control of glucose directly, using electronics rather than drugs," he says. "And the catalyst only activates when glucose levels are too high."

The approach also creates opportunities to connect medical treatments with digital technologies, including the Internet of Things. This refers to networks of devices that exchange information and respond automatically to changing conditions.

The researchers envision electronically controlled treatments that could be manufactured at scale and integrated with existing digital health systems.

Their next objective is to turn the experimental implant into a medical device suitable for further development and eventual clinical testing.

One potential advantage is its relatively simple glucose conversion mechanism. Because the catalyst does not rely on cells or enzymes, the researchers believe some of the technical challenges associated with biological treatments could be easier to overcome.

Much of the supporting technology is also already available. Wireless power transmission systems and external electronic controllers are commercially established, meaning the team would not need to develop every component from scratch.

If future studies demonstrate similar benefits in humans, this approach could open the door to a new class of diabetes treatments in which smart electronic devices help regulate blood sugar directly, potentially reducing reliance on conventional medications.

Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4477. Battlefield Labs is coming back for a short session to test out next week's Battlefield 6 update, and you can expect more tests in the future, too

Battlefield Labs is evolving, as it reopens its doors for its next - unusual - session.

Battlefield Studios is seemingly trying something different with Battlefield 6’s next patch, which everyone assumed would be a standard, mid-season update not intended to change the game significantly.

However, it appears that it may bring more to the game than we realised, enough that the developer sees it as an excuse to bring back the pre-launch Battlefield Labs testing initiative.

The December 9 patch kicks off the final phase of the game’s first season, which is set to take the game through the holidays and into the new year. We’ve known about its content for a while, and it’s definitely the lightest, compared to the two previous phases.

Battlefield Studios announced a host of new changes that will be included in the same patch, which are apparently significant enough to require player testing. The developer is reviving Battlefield Labs to help it do so, but only for three two-hour sessions, split across the game’s three main server regions (EU, NA, APAC).

All tests are scheduled for today, December 2, and they remain under NDA. Battlefield Labs is also sticking with PC as its chosen platform yet again, though you will be able to join through Steam this time, alongside the EA app.

The focus of the test will be on three key areas that the December 9 patch will be touching. First, there’s footstep audio, an issue that was really brought into focus with the launch of Redsec Battle Royale. You can expect to hear enemy footsteps from farther away, and intuitively know the type of surface they’re moving on.

The patch also brings another pass to hit registration and netcode, which BF Studios says should improve responsiveness in close-quarter situations. Finally, there are broader changes to other combat areas that the announcement didn’t elaborate on.

All testing will take place on Eastwood, and Operation Firestorm, rotating between Conquest, and Escalation.

Going forward, Battlefield Studios said to expect Labs to be open to more players, and for the process itself to be smoother. The developer wants to have faster turnaround times, after all, so that the initiative can test smaller changes and be more responsive to player feedback.

Some of the more involved, future sessions will include experiments with map layout changes and various other non-standard compositions of player and vehicle numbers. Of course, you can also expect new maps and modes to be tested in Labs, similar to how the CTE was used in Battlefield 4’s long life.

#4476. 8 JRPGs That Came Back From the Dead

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

It feels like we have been living through a game renaissance for quite some time. While development costs continue to inflate, particularly in the Western market, one way to keep the fanbase engaged with a developer and its IPs is to bet on smaller games, or even on ports, remasters, and remakes.

Another approach is to play on older fans' nostalgia, investing in older IPs while modernizing certain titles to attract newcomers at the same time. One genre that does this frequently is JRPGs, and as you can see in the following list, there are several JRPGs that pretty much came back from the dead, titles that had not shown their face in years and returned either as a remake or a brand new entry.

When Square Enix started with their HD-2D games, it was pure happiness. A rescue of the pixel art that the developer understands so well, but better than ever, paired with traditional gameplay. What I didn't expect, and I think nobody did, was that they would leverage this graphical engine to remake some older titles, and among these, Live A Live.

Live A Live was a JRPG released in 1994 for the Super Famicom exclusively in Japan, so imagine everyone's surprise when a modern remake was announced for 2022. Seriously, no one could have expected that. But there is a good reason, and aptly so, why Live A Live is timeless and was so well received by the modern audience 28 years after its original release.

Lunar was one of the JRPGs Game Arts released for the Sega CD, and it quickly earned a reputation as one of the finest JRPGs of the fourth generation. The first two mainline entries also quickly followed on PS1, reaching a much larger audience and becoming classic titles for the console. Portables followed, including Lunar Legend and the critically offensive Lunar Dragon Song.

In 2009, the series tried a comeback with Lunar: Silver Star Harmony, a remake of the first game for the PSP, and while critics loved it, it didn't give the franchise a second wind. Well, me, you, and our moms thought Lunar was over. But then, out of nowhere, GungHo announced Lunar Remastered Collection, a compilation of Lunar: Silver Star Story Complete and Lunar 2: Eternal Blue Complete, bringing the franchise back after 26 years without a sign of life.

Nihon Falcom is really focusing its efforts on bringing its entire lineup to modern platforms.

NISA is one of the oldest Japanese developers around, but the studio really found its footing after releasing the tactical La Pucelle: Tactics. It went on to mimic that gameplay style across several other franchises, mainly the well-known Disgaea. In 2004, it released Phantom Brave, another tactical JRPG following the same NISA blueprint, but with its own distinct identity and slightly different gameplay.

Phantom Brave was a solid game. I enjoyed it, but I really thought it was a one-and-done deal. I was pretty surprised when NISA announced Phantom Brave: The Lost Hero, not only a game set in the same universe, but a direct narrative sequel. Okay, luckily the game included a recap because releasing a sequel to a 20-year-old game was wild, but it is what it is.

I have mentioned Brigandine a few times here on the site, including in my review of Brigandine Abyss. I discovered this franchise serendipitously, and it took a long time to find other people who were also familiar with it. Truth be told, I only found them when I started frequenting the depths of Reddit. I had even forgotten about it, only to be reminded when I stumbled upon Brigandine: The Legend of Runersia.

Reviving an old IP or a cult classic happens every now and then, as you can see with other titles here. But Brigandine was not a cult hit, a classic, or even mildly famous. It was obscure among obscure titles, so why Happinet thought of bringing it back baffles me, but they did. Brigandine: The Legend of Forsena came out in 1998 and Runersia in 2020. The game apparently did well enough to warrant a new mainline entry, Brigandine Abyss, released just this year.

There are more than a few JRPGs that are still stuck on older systems and deserve a port to modern platforms.

I have always preferred fantasy games over sci-fi, but if there was one franchise where mechas stole my heart, or in this case, Wanzers, it was Front Mission. I played and replayed Front Mission 3 so many times and never grew tired of it, especially since the game featured branching narrative paths and a degree of RNG when learning skills, making every playthrough feel fresh. Then came the fourth mainline entry, Scars of War, Front Mission Evolved, and ugh, Left Alive, which come on, is not a Front Mission game, so let us dismiss it.

Well, in 2020, Forever Entertainment said it was working on a remake of an established Square Enix franchise that had multiple releases. My guess was either Parasite Eve or Front Mission, and since the former is tied up in licensing issues, yeah, it was Front Mission. The first remake launched in 2022, the second in 2023, and the third in 2025. I don't know if the franchise will continue, but it was great to revisit it through modern releases.

I know this entry is a bit far-fetched and even a tad insulting. After all, calling Valkyrie Elysium a mainline Valkyrie Profile entry is a stretch, but closing our eyes doesn't make it less true. After years without a new entry, Valkyrie Elysium was announced and left many fans excited, especially the nostalgic ones who adored the mysterious adventures of Lenneth back on the PS1.

What we got, however, wasn't what we wanted. It is not a bad game per se. It's just too middle-of-the-road and doesn't reflect what Valkyrie Profile represented, whether in the first game, Silmeria, or even Covenant of the Plume. Still, Valkyrie Elysium arrived in 2022, 13 years after the last mainline entry, so it fits the topic. I'm also not considering the mobile game Valkyrie Anatomia.

The producer is giving us hope, or at least some more coping issues.

Mana was always such a cozy, colorful, and friendly series. I loved playing Secret of Mana with my brother or transferring my character from Legend of Mana onto a memory card to bring to my friend's house. Good times. Even so, for one reason or another, it never achieved massive mainstream success. In 2007, Heroes of Mana came out for the Nintendo DS, followed in 2014 by Rise of Mana, a mobile-first game that received a Vita port. It was an oddity.

The franchise faded for a bit, but returned with the remake Adventures of Mana, followed by Secret of Mana and then Trials of Mana. The success of the remakes, especially Trials, signaled something to Square Enix, because it didn't take long for them to produce a brand-new mainline title in Visions of Mana. Personally, I loved Visions! It was a modernized version of everything I liked about Mana. I don't know why the game didn't achieve the success it deserved, but it may have been the last time we saw a mainline Mana entry.

You have probably heard someone say that Suikoden II is their favorite JRPG of all time. It was one of the most remarkable titles on the PS1 and built a deeply dedicated fanbase. Three more mainline entries later, the series began to fade into oblivion, still receiving a few spinoffs like Suikoden Tierkreis in 2009 and the Japan-only Gensō Suikoden: Tsumugareshi Hyakunen no Toki in 2012, which was its latest release. It was a strange era for both the series and Konami, which had stepped away from the video game industry for a while.

Then, completely out of nowhere, Konami announced Suikoden I & II HD Remaster: Gate Rune and Dunan Unification Wars during Tokyo Game Show 2022. It was a pleasant surprise, made even sweeter with the arrival of Suikoden Star Leap, which released in 2026. And okay, I know it is a mobile game, but those who played it (still locked in Japan) say it feels like a full-fledged Suikoden game, so who knows, maybe this will convince Konami to produce an offline version of Star Leap or a brand-new mainline entry altogether.

The GOG Dreamlist aims to preserve classic games. Here are 10 JRPGs that I would love to see on the platform, and they just need your vote.

#4475. Car Body Styles and Sizes Explained, from Compact Sedans to Full-Size SUVs and Everything in Between

If you’re looking understand the difference between a coupe and a sedan, or even between a compact SUV and a mid-size SUV, let us break it down.

The term "body style" is an all-encompassing label used to describe the size, shape, and characteristics of a vehicle. For example, sedans and pickup trucks are two popular vehicle body styles in the United States. At Car and Driver, we separate vehicles into eight primary body styles, making them easier to categorize (and easier for you to shop).

Within those eight broad body styles are a host of different variations that get even more specific. Size is one of the most important distinctions. We typically categorize vehicles in the following sizes, listed in increasing order: subcompact, compact, mid-size, and full-size. There are also differences in luxury vehicles versus non-luxury vehicles, and some vehicles that defy categorization altogether. Not sure where the car you’re interested in fits? We've broken down all of the main vehicle types and their subcategories to help you understand the body style basics.

See all results for used cars for sale near ?

Sedans are what most people picture when they think of a traditional passenger car. Sedans have four doors and incorporate a three-box design (jargon for a design with a distinct hood, passenger compartment, and trunk). Sedans come in multiple types and sizes, ranging from fuel-efficient and small compact to luxurious and large full-size options.

The smallest sedans in the U.S. are subcompact in size. Among non-luxury options, there are no sedans remaining in this segment, as automakers have dropped these entry-level options. The luxury subcompact segment is more flush with options. This subset includes the Audi A3 and Mercedes CLA-class.

Compact sedans are larger than subcompacts but smaller than mid-size models. Both mainstream and luxury options abound. In either form, compacts tend to offer reasonable space for cargo and people, though taller individuals may find these models’ rear seat room a bit too confining. The Honda Civic is a benchmark of the mainstream compact segment, as it expertly blends a reasonably roomy rear seat and trunk with enjoyable driving dynamics for a reasonable price. It’s why the model’s practically a regular on our 10Best Cars.

Mid-size sedans tend to sacrifice some of the driving enjoyment of their compact kin for additional rear seat and cargo space. These machines are perfect for those who regularly carry passengers or haul various items. The best mid-size sedans afford this extra versatility with only a marginal hit to behind-the-wheel joy. This includes the 10Best-winning Honda Accord in the mainstream segment and vehicles such as the BMW 5-series in the mid-size luxury segment.

Full-size sedans these days are the flagship models in a brand’s lineup. Only luxury-badged full-size sedans remain, as previous mainstream full-size options such as the Ford Taurus were discontinued years ago. The luxurious Mercedes-Benz S-class is a prime example of the category. Such sedans tend to emphasize a comfortable ride and loads of rear seat space above all else.

See all results for used cars for sale near ?

Sports sedans come in subcompact, compact, mid-size, and full-size forms. These models tend to be high-performance variants of more run-of-the-mill models, though some may argue that a number of these “run-of-the-mill” options are sports sedans in and of themselves. For instance, the subcompact Cadillac CT4 and compact Cadillac CT5 feature engaging rear-drive dynamics that arguably make these sedans worthy of the title. However, we limit the sports sedan designation to the models' truly sporty 10Best-winning CT4-V Blackwing and CT5-V Blackwing variants.

Sport utility vehicles, better known as SUVs, are the most popular vehicle type in the United States. This is in large part due to their versatility. Most SUVs offer generous space in the cabin and cargo area. They’re also offered in a variety of forms, from wagon-like crossover SUVs to hardcore off-road ones. Some are even capable of holding their own on the track.

Subcompact SUVs are the smallest of the breed. These typically inexpensive SUVs (relatively speaking, of course) often offer middling room for rear seat passengers or cargo, but do include the higher seating position and extra ground clearance that SUVs are associated with. Like their sedan stablemates, these models are available in both mainstream and luxury guises. While some subcompact SUVs feel more like penalty boxes, others, such as the 10Best-winning Chevrolet Trax, do a great job of making these entry-level machines feel anything but.

Compact SUVs—for example, the 10Best-winning Honda CR-V,—are effectively modern-day station wagons, combining reasonable rear seat and cargo space with a manageably sized footprint. Most mainstream compact SUVs are relatively affordable, and the best examples offer a versatile interior in a reasonably fun-to-drive package. On the other end of the spectrum, the 10Best-winning Porsche Macan trades interior space and versatility for dynamics that rival those of the best sports cars. In between sit luxury compact SUVs like the Genesis GV70, which combine luxurious wares with a comfortable ride and a generally playful chassis for once the roads start to turn.

Mid-size SUVs often have more passenger and cargo space. They also tend to offer a more premium feel, though both mainstream and luxury options are available. Some mid-size models offer just two rows of seats; while these choices offer the same five-passenger seating capacity as compact SUVs in most cases they have more space behind the rear seats for cargo when compared with a compact SUV. A prime example of a two-row, mid-size SUV is the Honda Passport.

Many mid-size SUVs are available with three rows of seats, providing seating for six, seven, or eight passengers depending on the configuration. The 10Best-winning Kia Telluride exemplifies the mid-size three-row category.

Full-size SUVs take advantage of their substantial dimensions, providing generous space for passengers and their stuff, as well as formidable towing capabilities. General Motors' Chevrolet Tahoe and GMC Yukon are two notable examples.

Crossover SUVs are available in all shapes and sizes, and many of the models we’ve already discussed are categorized as crossovers. Unlike traditional SUVs, which ride on truck-like body-on-frame underpinnings, crossover SUVs including the Honda CR-V use car-like unibody construction. The result is a vehicle that looks like an SUV (and in some instances, performs as well as an SUV—such as the Jeep Grand Cherokee and Land Rover Discovery) and offers the high seating position and—typically—the ground clearance of an SUV, but combines the maneuverability and ride comfort typically associated with cars.

Unlike traditional passenger cars that have a separate trunk around back, hatchbacks combine the passenger compartment and cargo hold into one continuous area. In place of a trunk lid, hatchbacks have a flip-up tailgate, called a "hatch," that can be raised to expose a large storage compartment behind the seats. Hatchbacks typically have either two or four passenger doors plus the hatch, which automakers often classify as an additional door.

The appeal of a rear hatch is rooted in practicality, and that is exactly what traditional hatchbacks are known for. Some models, like the Honda Civic, come in both sedan and hatchback body styles, the latter affording additional cargo volume.

Hot hatchbacks inject some adrenaline into the traditional hatchback formula. Models like the Volkswagen Golf R and Honda Civic Type R are fitted with potent engines and other go-fast features while retaining a rear hatch. That combination makes them equally usable for hefty grocery store runs and weekend track days.

Like sedans, coupes feature a three-box form. Unlike sedans, which feature four doors, coupes come with just two. Coupes tend to prioritize style over practicality, with attractive sloping roofs and limited rear passenger space.

Performance coupes sacrifice nearly everything in the name of high speeds and engaging handling. Two-seat sports cars like the Chevrolet Corvette and Porsche 911 GT3 RS also fall into the performance-coupe category, with mighty engines and sleek body lines being key pillars of the segment.

Luxury coupes take the two-door body style and up the extravagance with opulent cabins and high price tags. The Bentley Continental GT is an exemplar of the luxury-coupe class with quilted leather upholstery and sleek bodywork that oozes style.

In recent years, some automakers have started calling vehicles with sloping rooflines coupes, regardless of their door count or size. The Mercedes CLA-class is an example of a model that is marketed as a four-door coupe. Even some four-door SUVs, such as the BMW iX4, are sold as coupes despite the obvious contradictions.

Convertibles, often called droptops, feature a roof that folds (or drops) away into a compartment behind the passenger compartment for an unfettered view of the sky while cruising. Most convertibles have just two doors, but four-door options do exist. Some convertibles have electrically operated tops that tuck away at the push of a button, while others require the roof to be folded away and raised manually.

Softtop convertibles lack a solid roof and feature a canvas or fabric lid instead. These convertibles tend to weigh less than their hardtop-convertible counterparts.

Instead of using a soft material for the roof, hardtop convertibles feature hard body panels for a roof, which can be folded away—typically at the push of a button, as on the Chevrolet Corvette. Such a setup affords owners the benefits of open-air driving while allowing for additional protection from the elements with the roof in place, including outside noises.

Station wagons are a dying breed. Though they wear a similar shape to many squarebacked SUVs and crossovers, these typically lower-riding machines often share styling fore of the B-pillar (or from the front door forward) with an equivalent sedan in an automaker’s lineup. With no separate trunk and little to no peak in their roofline, station wagons offer a large and versatile cargo hold for hauling items of all sizes.

Luxury station wagons combine the niceties of an automaker's equivalent sedan and pair it with a more cargo-friendly wagon form.

Crossover station wagons, for instance the Audi A6 Allroad, take the basic wagon form and add a bit of (typically pseudo) off-road kit. This normally comes courtesy of unpainted plastic fascias and fender flares, a suspension lift, and standard all-wheel drive. Though these station wagons cannot replace a proper body-on-frame SUV with four-wheel drive off-road, they are capable of handling light off-tarmac terrains.

Pickup trucks are high-riding, utility-focused vehicles that feature a front passenger compartment (known as a "cab") and an open cargo bed in the rear. Most trucks offer some form of all-wheel drive system to improve their off-road and rough-weather capabilities. Pickups range in size from the compact and economical to big and heavy-duty.

Compact pickup trucks trade expansive cargo bed space for efficiency and versatility. While models like the 10Best-winning Ford Maverick and Hyundai Santa Cruz only have enough space in the back for hauling small loads, their small form factor and efficient engines grant them easy maneuverability and relatively impressive fuel economy.

Mid-size pickup trucks strike a balance between size, price, and capability. Mid-sizers such as the Toyota Tacoma and Ford Ranger typically have smaller beds and lower towing capacities than larger full-size and heavy-duty pickups; however, they trade this loss in capability for a smaller footprint and—often—a lower starting price.

Full-size pickup trucks are large and capable trucks with big beds and impressive tow ratings. They are ideal for serious work, but many full-size pickups, including the 10Best-winning Ram 1500 and Ford F-150, are comfortable enough for use as everyday vehicles.

As their name suggests, heavy-duty pickup trucks are meant for heavy hauling. HD workhorses, such as the Ram 2500 and 3500 HD and Ford F-250 and F-350 Super Duty, are easily capable of towing five-figure loads. HD pickups are often available with high-output diesel engines and can be optioned with different cab and bed sizes to suit the needs of multiple rugged professions.

Vans and minivans are known for their spacious insides and box-like exteriors. Both vans and smaller minivans are often long and tall, leaving a cavernous area behind the front seats for either passengers or cargo. Minivans almost unanimously come with one or more sliding rear doors, while bigger vans may include sliding rear doors or a pair of barn doors.

Cargo vans are made for hauling goods. Most come with just two seats, affording plenty of room for carrying cargo aft of the driver and front passenger. In many cases, cargo vans are used as commercial vehicles.

Passenger vans typically take the cargo van template but add a handful of extra exterior windows and multiple rows of rear seats to the mix. Passenger vans often serve as commercial vehicles, though those with a penchant for carrying many passengers will find lots to like in these machines, too.

As their name implies, minivans are, well, smaller-size vans. They're still plenty roomy, though, and typically offer seating for at least seven. With designs that maximize interior space, but a footprint comparable to a three-row mid-size SUV, minivans offer car-like comfort with loads of passenger and cargo room.

#4474. Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep

A major new scientific review is raising questions about whether medical cannabis actually helps people with insomnia. Despite growing interest in cannabis as a sleep treatment, researchers found that the available evidence is too weak to reliably determine whether it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or how well people function during the day.

Insomnia affects millions of people and can make it difficult to fall asleep, remain asleep throughout the night, or wake up feeling rested. Beyond the frustration of sleepless nights, the condition can seriously disrupt daily life and increase the likelihood of developing anxiety or depression.

Treatments for insomnia include cognitive behavioral therapy, which helps people change thoughts and habits that interfere with sleep, as well as medications such as antidepressants and antipsychotics. However, these approaches do not work equally well for everyone, fueling interest in alternative options.

Medical cannabis has attracted particular attention because of its potential to improve sleep. Unlike recreational cannabis, regulated medical products typically contain carefully measured amounts of THC and CBD, two compounds found in cannabis, and are administered as tablets, sprays, or oils. Despite its growing popularity, scientists have continued to debate whether cannabis offers meaningful benefits for people with insomnia.

Major Review Finds Little Evidence of Sleep Benefits

To investigate, researchers from The Cochrane Associate Centre at the Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires and the University of Manitoba examined nine clinical studies involving 537 adults between the ages of 18 and 76 who were receiving treatment for insomnia.

Most of the studies involved people with primary insomnia, meaning their sleep problems were not attributed to another medical condition. Eight trials compared regulated medical cannabis with a placebo, an inactive treatment used to measure whether a therapy produces genuine benefits. The remaining trial compared cannabis with amitriptyline, an antidepressant that is sometimes used to treat sleep problems.

Across the placebo comparisons, medical cannabis produced little or no clinically meaningful improvement in sleep quality, satisfaction with sleep, total hours slept, or daytime functioning.

The researchers also identified potential drawbacks. Participants who received medical cannabis were substantially more likely to experience mild side effects, including dizziness and dry mouth, than those given a placebo. However, this finding came from a relatively small number of studies, limiting confidence in the result.

There was some indication that medical cannabis might improve overall quality of life. Yet the evidence supporting this possibility was highly uncertain. When the findings were combined, the results were consistent with outcomes ranging from a slight decline in quality of life to a substantial improvement.

"The main message is that the research currently available is not sufficient to reliably answer whether medical cannabis helps people with insomnia," says Dr. Lucia Varela, lead author of the study from the University of Manitoba, Canada. "This does not mean that medical cannabis is ineffective. It means that, based on the evidence we have, we cannot draw reliable conclusions about its effectiveness for insomnia in the general population."

Why Scientists Remain Uncertain About Cannabis and Insomnia

One of the biggest problems was the quality of the research itself. The reviewers rated their confidence in the available evidence as low or very low, citing small study populations, conflicting findings, and potential bias in how the trials were conducted.

Another challenge was the lack of consistency between studies. Researchers tested different medical cannabis products, making it difficult to directly compare their results or determine whether particular formulations might work better than others.

The studies were also relatively short. The longest followed participants for just 12 weeks, leaving major unanswered questions about whether medical cannabis could provide lasting sleep benefits or produce additional effects with prolonged use.

More Research Is Needed Before Cannabis Can Be Recommended

The researchers also cautioned that the study participants did not adequately represent the broader population of people living with insomnia.

Women accounted for nearly three-quarters (72.66% of participants), and the research was heavily weighted toward younger adults. As a result, it remains unclear whether the findings would apply equally to men, older individuals, or people whose insomnia occurs alongside other medical conditions.

Taken together, these limitations mean that the existing research cannot establish whether medical cannabis is an effective insomnia treatment. The authors emphasize that larger, more rigorous clinical trials are needed before it can be confidently recommended for improving sleep.

Importantly, the findings do not establish that medical cannabis is ineffective. Instead, they highlight how much remains unknown about a treatment that has gained considerable attention despite limited high-quality evidence.

"The evidence is too weak and uncertain to draw firm conclusions about the use of medical cannabis for insomnia," says Dr. Luis Garegnani, senior author from Universidad Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires, Argentina. "Rather than viewing the findings as either an endorsement or a rejection of medical cannabis, clinicians and patients should recognize the uncertainty and consider individual circumstances while better evidence is generated."

HoYoverse just hosted a sizeable Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, revealing more than just the game’s next major update. Version 3.8 was the big highlight, of course, with the new release arriving soon, on December 16-17 depending on your server region.

Alongside showing everything coming with this next update, the developer also announced that 3.8 will go on for eight weeks, rather than the usual six. V3.8 is dubbed "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams", and it brings an end to the Amphoreus journey.

The story in "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams" takes place after the final battle of Amphoreus, where Constance "The Dahlia" appears to deliver a twist: the Trailblazer's memories are scattered, with many parts missing.

This final quest revolves around finding them in order to piece together the mystery, and involves a return to Penacony. This memory-hunting adventure is told from the perspective of Firefly, which will also explain how she entered the dreamscape initially and met the squad.

The new playable character is The Dahlia, whose power is linked to the the Remembrance path, which allows her to fabricate memories. Despite taking her powers from the Remembrance, The Dhalia actually follows the Path of Nihility in-game: she’s a 5-Star character who shines in teams dealing Break DMG.

The Dhalia can unleash a Gloomy Zone that causes Toughness Reduction inflicted by allies to trigger Super Break DMG, even before you break your enemies’ Weaknesses. The Dahlia can also invite one teammate to become her Dance Partner, which allows them (and her) to deal additional Super Break DMG each time they attack an enemy. If you trigger her Ultimate after picking a Dance Partner, she applies Type Weaknesses of both partners to enemies.

While The Dahlia is the only new character appearing in this final Amphoreus update, there'll be reruns aplenty, with an unusual third banner phase to make up for the extra long wait for 4.0. Appropriately for her role in the story, Firefly will make her return alongside The Dahlia in Phase 1, while Fugue and Lingsha will both have banner reruns in Phase 2, which is expected on January 7th. A bonus two-week-long Phase 3 will then begin on January 28th, seeing brief reappearances for popular returning characters Aglaea and Sunday, before things (presumably) go back to normal with the new annual update.

Something else to look forward to in 3.8 is The Chrysos Awoo Championship, which invites players to become chimera trainers and compete in team-based battles. The Remnants of Twilight event kicks off with the new patch, too, featuring its own set of challenges. However, HoYoverse have confirmed that there won't be an extra event during Phase 3 — but hopefully that'll give you some time to wrap up the last of the Amphoreus story content, which is longer than the previous four chapters put together.

#4470. Tomorrow’s Battlefield 6 patch is the first step towards improving footstep audio, and it might actually fix the settings reset bug

The next major Battlefield 6 patch is nearly upon us, and Battlefield Studios is promising a bounty of changes - including a couple of fixes to some big bugs.

Battlefield 6 is about to receive a new update. Version 1.1.3.0 is set to arrive tomorrow, December 9 to kick off the third and final phase of the game’s first season. Winter Offensive brings some holiday-themed new content to the game, but it’s not the most interesting part of the patch.

That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the new patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.

Thew new content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly. To go along with that there are new limited-time modes for both multiplayer and Redsec’s Gauntlet. The event mode will be available in Conquest, and Domination.

The Ice Climbing Axe is the only new weapon in this drop. The battle pass gets a new Winter Offensive bonus path, just like we’ve seen with previous seasonal stages. This is how you unlock the axe, too.

Easily the most interesting change in this update is the range of improvements to audio across the board. First, footstep audio received a big pass that should make it easier to hear enemy footsteps, easier to locate them, and across different surfaces.

Some of the bugs that caused certain sounds to simply vanish have been fixed. This was especially prevalent in battle royale matches. BF Studios explained in the patch notes that it has adjusted memory priorities for in-game sounds in order to prioritise the most crucial ones. This is not the end of the road on audio, however, as the developer continues to work on making the soundscape more stable and reliable.

Some of those audio changes are the result of recent testing done in Battlefield Labs, which is also responsible for another exciting addition in this latest patch: improvements to hit registration.

While BF6 has had solid and stable netcode, certain situations would sometimes create uncertainty about how you died, and why certain actions seemingly failed to perform at that particular moment.

The focus in this update is to improve the reliability of how actions in close-quarter combat are translated, which includes firing before fully going into ADS, quick aim changes and more.

Speaking of close-range, the patch also brings another pass to soldier visibility to make it easier for enemies to stand out from the background. This is particularly relevant in areas with low contrast, or busy environments with lots of particle and visual effects.

1.1.3.0 also brings yet another set of weapon handling and gunplay tweaks, this time focusing on accuracy issues with first shots. You can also expect more tweaks to attachment behaviour with regards to recoil.

Something else worth highlighting is that vehicle gameplay is getting several smaller tweaks that have to do with how they interact with the world, how their HUDs behave and more. Finally, your settings should no longer be reset after applying an update. BF Studios says there are still some instances where that might happen, but the issue should be fixed for the majority of players.

You can read the full change log on the Battlefield blog.

#4469. Even moderate drinking linked to cancer and early death, major study finds

A major new study suggests that even modest amounts of alcohol may carry serious health consequences. Researchers found that drinking levels many Americans consider moderate are associated with higher risks of premature death, disability, cancer, heart disease, and other long-term health problems.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research challenges the longstanding belief that moderate drinking is harmless or may even provide health benefits. The findings suggest that alcohol's risks begin at relatively low levels of consumption and increase as people drink more.

"This study provides the most comprehensive U.S. estimates to date of lifetime risks of alcohol-attributable mortality and morbidity, showing that even moderate levels of consumption increase the risk of premature death and disability," said study co-author Katherine M. Keyes, PhD, professor of Epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

"No protective effect of drinking was observed even at low levels," added Keyes, whose research examines alcohol and other substance use across different stages of life.

"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," said lead study author Kevin Shield, PhD, an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."

Major Study Examines the Lifetime Health Risks of Alcohol

To better understand how drinking affects health over a lifetime, researchers from the United States and Canada conducted an extensive review of existing scientific evidence.

Medical experts evaluated more than 7,200 scientific articles examining diseases and injuries associated with alcohol consumption. They used this evidence to determine how drinking influences the risk of individual health conditions, then combined those findings with large national health data sets.

Using statistical models, the team estimated how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious illnesses or dying prematurely over a lifetime.

The analysis covered a wide range of health problems linked to alcohol, including cardiovascular disease, liver disease, injuries, and several forms of cancer. Among the cancers examined were those affecting the esophagus, mouth, and breast.

By considering these conditions together, the researchers were able to estimate alcohol's overall health burden rather than focusing on individual diseases.

Why Two Drinks a Day May Be Riskier Than You Think

One of the study's most important findings concerns drinking habits that many people would not consider excessive.

Consuming two alcoholic drinks per day, a level often viewed as socially moderate, was associated with a substantially higher risk of premature death attributable to alcohol.

The findings also provide more specific information than the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines, which recommend that Americans "limit alcoholic beverages" but do not identify a particular amount that can be consumed safely.

Earlier dietary recommendations set daily limits of two alcoholic drinks for men and one for women. However, what counts as a single drink depends on the beverage and its alcohol content. A standard drink generally corresponds to 12 ounces of beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits, although differences in alcohol concentration can change those amounts.

According to the researchers, the newer guidelines communicate a useful 'less-is-best' principle but lack specific numerical estimates that would help people understand how health risks change with consumption.

Their analysis was intended to fill that gap by measuring risks across a broad range of drinking levels.

Does Moderate Drinking Have Any Health Benefits?

For years, moderate alcohol consumption has sometimes been promoted as beneficial for cardiovascular health. The new findings cast doubt on that idea when the full range of alcohol-related health effects is considered.

The researchers found no statistically significant protective effect on overall health at any level of alcohol consumption.

They acknowledged that relatively low alcohol intake may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. Ischemic heart disease occurs when reduced blood flow deprives the heart muscle of the oxygen it needs, often because arteries have narrowed or become blocked.

However, any potential cardiovascular benefits must be considered alongside alcohol's association with cancer, liver disease, injuries, and other serious conditions.

When the researchers combined these outcomes, the potential benefits were outweighed by the harmful effects, even among people consuming seven alcoholic drinks per week.

This broader assessment helps explain why a drinking habit that appears beneficial when examining one disease may still increase overall health risks.

Although the findings offer a clearer picture of the long-term dangers of alcohol, the researchers emphasize that the estimates describe risks across populations, not the precise likelihood that any individual will develop a particular disease.

The statistical models relied on "the best possible data," according to the research team. Nevertheless, personal health outcomes can differ considerably depending on genetics, lifestyle, drinking patterns, and other individual factors.

To calculate the overall burden of alcohol consumption, the investigators estimated risks for health conditions already known to have a causal relationship with drinking. They then combined those estimates to assess the total impact.

The researchers also acknowledged that scientific understanding of alcohol's health effects continues to evolve. Emerging evidence suggests that drinking may be associated with additional conditions, including pancreatic cancer, that require further investigation.

"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," said Keyes and Shield.

Despite these uncertainties, the results offer an important reference point: alcohol consumption above one drink per day was associated with increased health risks for both men and women.

The researchers believe that giving people more specific information about these risks can help them make better decisions about how much they drink.

"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking."

Why the Findings Matter for U.S. Alcohol Guidelines

The research also raises questions about how scientific evidence is considered when federal drinking recommendations are developed.

In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former associate administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, discussed the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the federal dietary guidance process.

"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."

Vincent's comments highlight concerns about whether the research received appropriate consideration during the development of national recommendations.

The study's findings reinforce the importance of understanding alcohol's cumulative health effects rather than assuming that moderate consumption is beneficial or risk-free. Although individual risks vary, the overall pattern was clear: greater alcohol consumption was associated with greater harm, and the researchers found no overall health advantage to drinking.

The research was funded by Synergy Enterprises Inc. and the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

#4468. 2027 Lamborghini Temerario

See all results for new 2027 Lamborghini Temerario for sale near 29405

The Temerario might be the runt of the Lamborghini supercar litter, but it's still one raging bull. Taking the reins from its widely lauded Huracan predecessor, the Temerario is the least expensive way into Lambo's supercar lineup, but it doesn’t sacrifice much performance compared to the company's Revuelto flagship—in fact, it beats its brawnier older brother to 60 mph by a tenth of a second.

Under the Temerario's origami-folded sheetmetal lies a newly developed 4.0-liter twin-turbo V-8 nestled into the car's aluminum spaceframe just ahead of the rear axle. As if 789 horsepower from the engine alone wasn’t enough, a trio of electric motors—one mounted between the engine and transmission and one at each front wheel—ups its total output to 907 Italian stallions. If you somehow tire of the sound of the flat-plane-crank V-8's goosebump-raising 10,000-rpm wail, the electric motors also allow for short periods of silent, all-electric driving. With its mighty hybrid-assisted thrust, poster-worthy looks, and agile moves, the Temerario is every inch a purebred Lambo and well worthy of supercar status.

Expert Tip: If you'd rather have a horse instead of a bull in your garage, the Ferrari 296GTB is a steed with the need for speed, and moves to match the Lambo for a similar price.

Compare the 2027 Lamborghini Temerario with the top vehicles in this segment with our new compare tool.

Lamborghini's newest bull debuted in 2026 and charges into 2027 without any notable changes.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

The Temerario's powertrain consists of a twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8 with a flat-plane crankshaft, a trio of axial-flux electric motors, and an eight-speed dual-clutch transmission. The Temerario's V-8 alone is good for 789 horsepower; adding the output of the three electric motors brings the total combined output to 907 horsepower. That's just 94 ponies shy of the Lamborghini Revuelto, the brand's V-12 halo car. On the Temerario, one electric motor mounts to the V-8 in front of the transmission, while the remaining two live up front, one at each wheel. The Temerario's V-8 redlines at 10,000 rpm, and the engine's peak torque of 538 pound-feet is available from 4000 to 7000 rpm. While the flat-plane-crank V-8 sounds glorious when pushed to its limit, we wish that its exhaust packed a bit more fury earlier in the rev range.

With the electric motors in play, maximum torque output rises to 590 pound-feet. In addition to supplying enormous power, the hybrid configuration helps provide instantaneous torque and linear power delivery over a broad range of speeds and driving situations. Thirteen drive programs are available via a rotary button on the steering wheel, including launch and drift modes, the latter offering three levels of tail-out leeway. We drove the Temerario at the track and on the street and were enthralled with its lively powertrain and playful demeanor.

Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.

In Comparison: In our testing, the Temerario got to 60 mph in a ridiculously quick 2.1 seconds. It also ripped through the quarter-mile in 9.4 seconds at 150 miles per hour. Both figures beat its big sibling, the Revuelto, by 0.3 seconds and 2 mph, respectively.

Juice is stored in a 3.8-kWh lithium-ion battery pack. The battery resides in the center tunnel along with the transmission—the location is said to help optimize weight distribution and is protected from underneath by structural elements. Regenerative braking and power from the internal-combustion engine both replenish the battery's state of charge. Plug-in charging is also possible via a standard 7-kW onboard charger; with typical household current, it can recharge an empty battery to full capacity in a claimed 30 minutes. An EV-only mode provides around 4 miles of range.

The EPA estimates that the Temerario will deliver 14 mpg city, 19 mpg highway, and 16 mpg combined. When we get a chance to test the Temerario, we'll update this story with results from our 75-mph highway fuel economy test. For more information about the Temerario's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

First Row: Thanks to its all-aluminum chassis, the Temerario's interior offers more space than the Huracán it replaced. Headroom increased by 1.3 inches, legroom by 1.8 inches, and Lamborghini claims the interior is large enough to accommodate drivers up to six feet five wearing a helmet. The interior shares some styling cues from the Revuelto; four stitching patterns are available, and the 18-way adjustable driver's seat is heated and ventilated. The Temerario also borrows the Revuelto's steering wheel, which is too busy with controls for our liking.

Cargo Capacity: If you're planning on taking the Temerario on a weekend getaway, you'd better pack light; the front trunk only has a four-cubic-foot capacity.

Lamborghini says the Temerario offers the most advanced suite of infotainment and connectivity features of any model in its lineup. Three displays—a 12.3-inch instrument panel with three user-selectable views, an 8.4-inch infotainment screen, and a 9.1-inch passenger screen—occupy prime dashboard real estate. Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are standard, as is a Sonus Faber audio system.

The most notable feature, though, is the optional Lamborghini Vision Unit (LAVU) system. Essentially an on-board data acquisition system, the setup utilizes three cameras: one viewing the road, one focused on the passengers, and one looking forward over the driver's shoulder. Preloaded with data for 150 different racing circuits, the system can be used to evaluate and improve driver performance. It also enables a "memories recorder" function that allows for up to two minutes of off-track recording, and works as a dashcam that can capture one minute of incident history.

Compared to most other cars, the Temerario doesn't offer many driver-assistance features.

#4467. Mercedes Delays U.S. GLC Production, Leaving the Model Vulnerable to Tariffs

The brand’s bread-and-butter crossover won’t be made in the United States until the next generation launches.

Mercedes-Benz is delaying the start of its U.S. production of the GLC-class crossover, according to Automotive News. The automaker had originally planned for production of the GLC to begin in late 2027, but the paper reports that it has now been delayed to 2030. When the U.S. production does begin, it will take place at the automaker’s Vance, Alabama, plant.

According to the AN report, Mercedes is delaying the move in production to wait for the arrival of the next-generation GLC-class. “Investing in the plant for about half a life cycle and then having to retool for the next-generation GLC doesn’t make a lot of sense financially,” Sam Fiorani, the vice president of AutoForecast, told the outlet. The Alabama plant, in its current configuration, is home to the GLS-class and GLE-class SUVs, along with their electric counterparts.

See all results for new 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLC-Class for sale near 94043

The updated timeline lines up with the expected arrival of the next-generation GLC-class; the current model received its most recent refresh in 2023. Unfortunately, the delay leaves the GLC-class, which is one of the most important models for the brand in the United States, exposed to increased costs related to import tariffs. Mercedes has previously committed to spending some $4 billion at its Alabama plant to localize the production of its high-volume vehicles, which are currently subject to 15 percent import tariffs.

On the flip side, some reports suggest that the Trump administration is considering lowering its tariff on European cars to 10 percent in an attempt to sway Audi into building a planned $4 billion Georgia plant. Car and Driver reached out to Mercedes-Benz for confirmation of the AN report but has not heard back at the time of this article’s publication. We will update this story when we learn more.

#4466. Fragmentary Order Looks Like Sci-Fi Escape from Tarkov, And You Can Play It This Year

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

If you've ever wondered what Escape from Tarkov would look like if its brutal firefights took place somewhere beyond Earth, Nikita Buyanov might have just the answer. The game director behind the popular hardcore shooter has finally offered a proper look at his next project, and it seems he's not planning to make things any easier for players.

Called Fragmentary Order, the upcoming sci-fi tactical shooter just received its first gameplay reveal, featuring an impressive 14 minutes of in-engine footage. And if you're curious to see what Buyanov has been working on, you can watch the full gameplay reveal on YouTube!

Escape From Tarkov's creator reveals that his upcoming game is 'almost there.'

Set across the Solar System in 2251, Fragmentary Order imagines a future where warfare has become an outsourced business. So, instead of putting their own lives on the line, players control remotely operated clones known as RepEnts, which are deployed across large combat zones to carry out all sorts of dangerous missions.

Interestingly, losing one of these clones isn't necessarily the end of the road. In this world, death is simply another business expense, but that doesn't mean players can afford to be careless. The game features large-scale environments, changing environmental conditions, vehicles, drones, and advanced technological systems, with squads of up to four players expected to coordinate their operations.

If you've ever wondered what Escape from Tarkov would look like if its brutal firefights took place somewhere beyond Earth, Nikita Buyanov might have just the answer.

Buyanov is also taking a more grounded approach to its sci-fi setting (as you should expect from the same mind that created Escape From Tarkov). Rather than relying on futuristic gimmicks like wall-hacks, the upcoming hardcore shooter features electromagnetic sensors that can expose players' positions, meaning every encounter requires careful planning and an understanding of the battlefield. In other words, running around without thinking twice probably won't get you very far!

Battlestate Games boss Nikita Buyanov opens up about his creative vision for his upcoming game, Fragmentary Order.

Alongside the gameplay reveal, Buyanov also announced “Prime Batch”, a paid program that gives players access to the game's upcoming closed testing sessions. So yes, some dedicated fans won't have to wait until the game's full release to get their hands on it, as closed testing sessions are expected to begin later this year.

There are two available tiers: Candidate ($44.99), which includes access to alpha sessions and major technical playtests, and Founder ($79.99), which adds earlier access to experimental builds, roadmap updates, and a private community with direct developer access. The first closed alpha wave is planned for later this year, and you can check out more about it on this page.

For now, Fragmentary Order doesn't have a confirmed release date, but its first gameplay showcase has certainly given fans plenty to discuss. If Buyanov manages to capture the same long-term appeal that made Escape from Tarkov so popular while introducing a compelling sci-fi setting, his next project could be one worth keeping an eye on.

Fragmentary Order is a next-generation multiplayer combat tactical simulator.

#4465. Drinking tea may help protect your heart, but there’s a surprising catch

Drinking tea regularly may offer important benefits for your heart and blood vessels, according to a massive study involving nearly 500,000 adults. Researchers found that people who consumed tea regularly had a lower risk of developing several vascular diseases compared with those who did not drink tea.

However, the findings also revealed some unexpected differences. The type of tea, how strong it was, and even the temperature at which it was consumed were all associated with vascular health. While certain tea drinking habits were linked to a lower risk of disease, drinking tea at extremely high temperatures appeared to have the opposite association.

The research, published in the Journal of Internal Medicine, provides new insights into how an everyday beverage may be connected to long-term cardiovascular health.

Nearly 500,000 Adults Reveal a Link Between Tea and Vascular Health

The study included 485,934 adults in China who were followed for a median of 9.05 years. During that period, researchers recorded 14,863 cases involving several types of vascular disease.

These conditions included cardiovascular disease, which affects the heart and blood vessels, and cerebrovascular disease, which involves blood vessels that supply the brain. The researchers also examined pulmonary heart disease, a condition in which problems involving the lungs or their blood vessels place strain on the heart, and peripheral artery disease, which occurs when arteries carrying blood to areas such as the legs become narrowed or blocked.

Although these conditions affect different parts of the body, they share an important feature: they interfere with the circulation of blood, which delivers oxygen and nutrients to organs and tissues.

When the researchers compared tea drinking habits with the incidence of these diseases, they found that regular tea consumption was associated with an 11% lower risk of the combined vascular outcomes.

The relationship also appeared to vary with the amount consumed. Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk occurred at approximately six to eight cups per day.

This does not necessarily mean that drinking more tea directly prevents disease or that everyone should consume that amount. Because the research was observational, it could identify connections between tea drinking and health outcomes but could not establish that tea itself was responsible for the differences.

Black Tea vs. Green Tea: Does the Type Matter?

One particularly interesting finding involved the type of tea participants consumed.

Black tea showed more consistent associations with a reduced risk of vascular disease than green tea. This suggests that different varieties of tea may not have identical relationships with cardiovascular health.

Both black and green tea come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis, but they undergo different processing methods. Black tea is typically allowed to undergo extensive oxidation, a chemical process that changes the composition of compounds in the leaves, while green tea is processed to limit oxidation.

Tea naturally contains plant compounds known as polyphenols, which have attracted scientific interest because of their antioxidant properties and potential effects on blood vessel function. Antioxidants can help limit certain types of cellular damage caused by reactive molecules.

However, the study does not establish whether these compounds explain the observed differences between black and green tea.

Tea strength also appeared to matter. Participants who drank tea of moderate strength had the lowest associated vascular disease risk, suggesting that stronger tea was not necessarily linked to greater benefits.

Drinking Tea Too Hot May Carry Unexpected Risks

Perhaps the most surprising finding concerned tea temperature.

Although regular tea consumption was generally associated with a reduced risk of vascular disease, drinking tea described as "burning hot" was linked to an increased risk.

The result suggests that the temperature of tea may be an important consideration alongside how much people drink and which variety they prefer.

Very hot beverages can expose tissues in the mouth and digestive tract to high temperatures, but the study did not establish the biological mechanism behind the observed vascular risk. It also did not identify a specific temperature at which tea becomes harmful.

The findings therefore should not be interpreted as proof that drinking extremely hot tea directly causes vascular disease. They do, however, raise questions about whether certain drinking habits could offset some of the favorable associations seen with regular tea consumption.

Tea, Exercise, and Smoking Habits May Work Together

The researchers also examined how tea consumption related to other lifestyle factors, including smoking and physical activity.

Their analysis showed that people who regularly drank tea, were not current smokers, and maintained high levels of physical activity had the lowest vascular disease risk.

"Joint analyses showed that tea consumption, smoking status and physical were collectively associated with vascular risk, with the favorable combination of habitual tea consumption, non-current smoking and high physical activity associated with the lowest risk," the authors wrote.

These results highlight the importance of considering overall lifestyle rather than looking at a single food or beverage in isolation.

Regular physical activity supports cardiovascular health in several ways, including improving circulation, helping regulate blood pressure, and supporting the function of the heart and blood vessels. Avoiding smoking also reduces exposure to substances that can damage blood vessels and increase cardiovascular risk.

Taken together, the findings suggest that tea drinking may be one component of a broader pattern of habits associated with better vascular health.

Although more research is needed to determine whether tea consumption directly influences disease risk, the study offers encouraging evidence that this widely consumed beverage is associated with cardiovascular health. It also highlights an important distinction: when it comes to tea, the amount, variety, strength, and temperature may all be worth considering.

#4461. Driven: The Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Won’t Make You Wait

The Mercedes-AMG GT55 and GT63 EVs bring Formula 1 battery technology to the road.

The most shocking thing about the new Mercedes-AMG GT63 4-Door Coupe isn’t its 1475 pound-feet of torque or its 1153 horsepower. Or the estimated 2.0-second run to 60 mph. Or the flat cornering. Or the responsive steering. Or the drive modes that let you change how the GT doles out its three-motor grunt. It isn’t even the polarizing style. It’s that this car charges at at a rate of up to 600 kilowatts.

That kind of power makes replenishing the battery almost as quick as pumping gas. Mercedes says its new GT will go from 10 to 80 percent in just 11 minutes. In a demonstration we witnessed, the car was still pulling 259 kilowatts at 78 percent state of charge. Impressive stuff.

Of course, finding a 600-kW charger in the U.S. is another story. In Europe, these kinds of high-high-power DC chargers are increasing in popularity thanks to a growing quantity of heavy electric trucks. But even if you can’t find a charger that can provide more than 350 kW of juice, the GT63—and its less powerful sibling, the 805-hp GT55—can max that charger out for much longer than an EV with a 350-kW peak. As you might expect, both GT variants will come to the U.S. with NACS plugs.

See all results for new 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door EV for sale near 33186

The 2027 GT 4-Door can do this thanks to a thermal strategy borrowed from Formula 1. The car’s 106-kWh battery pack, which consists of 2660 cells arranged in 18 modules, is oil cooled. The terminals of the individual cells are where the heat really builds during charging, and by using a cooling loop that focuses on those terminals first, engineers can pump more power into the battery without damaging the cells. This method keeps temps stable across the entire battery within a range of about 9 degrees.

EPA ranges are still TBD, but we expect both the GT55 and GT63 to break 300 miles in maximum-range configuration. Wheels and tires will play a role as they always do, but we mention a max-range config because the GT 4-Door packs a couple of optional active aerodynamic elements to boost range. A hidden front panel works in concert with an extendable rear diffuser, because extending the body’s total length reduces drag. (It’s also really interesting when the diffuser extends several inches beyond the rear bumper.) There are also some moving elements under the body work that increase downforce, but those are more for corner carving than for hypermiling. And, of course, the wing out back can adjust to reduce drag or increase downforce, depending on driving behavior.

The higher-zoot GT63 also comes packed with all manner of newfangled suspension hardware. Hydraulic anti-roll control and air springs support multilink geometries front and rear. All the suspension components are aluminum, except for the two rear upper links, which are stamped steel. The lower-power 55 gets conventional anti-roll bars instead of the hydraulic ones. Rear-axle steer, which can turn the rear rollers up to 6 degrees in either direction, is standard.

See all results for new 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door EV for sale near 33186

Another clever addition is the use of aramid in the crash structure, a synthetic fiber you might recognize from its use in bulletproof vests. AMG lashes aramid rope (roughly the diameter of a hearty man’s pinkie finger) to the longitudinal chassis rails. In the event that the car hits a pole or a tree, the rope transfers the load to the chassis, and those longitudinal members crumple inward a bit, hopefully preventing the impact from involving the undoubtedly expensive front motor.

“Structural frunk” is a phrase we’re still getting used to saying out loud. The AMG GT 4-Door has a small frunk, yes, but it’s best used to store a charging cable or other small knickknacks you want to keep handy. Unlike your typical plastic frunk, though, this one is made of carbon fiber. The box bolts directly to the chassis, and it’s stiff enough that it boosts the torsional rigidity of the front end by 35 percent. It is also curved to direct airflow under the hood, so it has three purposes. (Serving as an ersatz beverage cooler does not count as a fourth.)

The AMG Dynamic Package, which is standard on the GT63 and optional on the GT55, brings three control knobs labeled Response, Agility, and Traction to the center console. These knobs, called Race Engineer, have a profound effect on the car’s behavior. The Response knob, available in all drive modes, plays with the accelerator calibration. Position one is a very lazy “throttle”; acceleration ramps up almost comically slowly. On the other side, position nine is a light switch. The Agility knob, which is only active in Sport, Sport+, and Race modes with stability control turned off, works in concert with what remains of the stability control, the front-to-rear torque split, and the rear-axle torque vectoring. Position one maintains a tight line, while nine allows for lurid drifts. The Traction knob, also only active in Sport, Sport+, and Race modes with stability control turned off, is pretty self-explanatory; nine almost eliminates the traction assist entirely.

Tinkering with these three knobs generates vastly different results. If you want to work on your driving line around a track, keep the Agility and Response knobs in positions one through three. The car keeps the body tight and perfectly meters power on corner exit. Crank them to seven or higher, and you’ll meet your new best friend: oversteer. Just mash the throttle and keep the front tires pointed where you want to go, and Race Engineer will handle the rest.

Sport+ is the only mode where fake powertrain sounds are pumped into the cabin. In addition to that synthetic soundtrack, a tachometer appears on the instrument screen, and the steering-wheel paddles change jobs from adjusting brake-regen levels to working virtual gears. The V-8 rumble, which includes shakers in the front seats, is based on the last-gen AMG GT R and manages a solid impersonation. Shifts arrive with an abrupt but brief interruption in torque; sure, the feeling is probably more pronounced than what’s felt from the actual GT R’s dual-clutch, but the theatrics are executed perfectly.

With the Agility and Response knobs set to seven, the GT63 drives much smaller than its 119.7-inch wheelbase and 5500-pound curb weight imply. Turn-in is crisp, and adroit steering corrections result in quick responses. You can even trail-brake this big car deep into corners while the Race Engineer algorithms help with rotation.

Driving around town, the GT55 is limited to 557 horses and the GT63 to 711, but a quick hop over to Race mode will call up all the remaining horses. Should you desire short periods of naughty driving, a boost mode achieves the same full-power blast, albeit in 55- and 63-second bursts (you can guess which model gets which duration). It’s not like you need four figures’ worth of horsepower to make a pass on a mountain road, but passengers will surely love it. Both variants are quiet and smooth riding, though not quite as smooth as an Active Ride–equipped Porsche Taycan.

Figuring out where the AMG lands among other high-power EV sedans will have to wait for a comparison test, but our first sampling indicates that the Merc splits the difference between the more spacious Lucid Air and the smaller Taycan. The GT’s interior is top-spec Mercedes, full of great materials and clever ergonomic touches. There’s a fair amount of customization through the central display, our favorite of which is the ability to rearrange and even hide some of the functions on the steering wheel knobs. Residents of Phoenix, for example, can remove Slippery mode from the mode-switching dial. Degenerates can set the dial to only include Comfort and Race. The sky’s the limit.

The 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT55 goes on sale later this year with a starting price of $146,550, undercutting the driver-focused Taycan GTS. When the 63 hits dealers next year for $176,550, it’ll likewise undercut on the Porsche Taycan Turbo. With this level of performance on board—both the charging and the hard-charging kind—the GT 4-Door should be quite a strong competitor.
